missions.title: The Doorway Pause
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How does the timing of an action shape the reason an audience sees in it?
missions.stake: If the programme says more than a seat can see, the audience leaves sure of something it never saw.

objectives.title: Follow the passage to the House of Performance.
Run both cue orders and compare the timing with Director Edda.
Read the blocking plan and gallery sightline with Host Hari.
Choose the cue order for tonight’s scene.

onComplete.checkpoint: House of Performance: cue order chosen

objectives.title: Read the audience’s note after the show.
Help Hari keep the movement and the audience’s reading distinct in the program.

missions.title: A Copy for the Understudy
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What does another performer need in order to try a staging they did not see?

objectives.title: Make a cue copy the understudy can use from the rehearsal bench.

missions.title: A Rule by the Door
missions.knowledgeQuestion: When can a record settle what waiting at a door means?

objectives.title: Find the signed admission register in the City of Copies.
Take the admission register’s line to the hall door or the returns queue.

missions.title: The Seat before the Bell
missions.knowledgeQuestion: Who gets to use a room when its usual rules give people different starting points?

objectives.title: Check the folded seat request and try the other queue-post location.
Set out a seating notice that keeps the aisle clear.

missions.title: The Call at the Side Bench
missions.stake: The first people through the door may hear a verdict about the keeper before they see the scene.
missions.knowledgeQuestion: Whose words reach the audience before an actor speaks?

objectives.title: Set a cue for the part of the move the post hides. Check what reaches the listeners.

missions.title: The Same Door in Two Lights
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What can a way of showing a moment teach someone about the moment?

objectives.title: Try both lights on the same relief and read the dated maker’s slip.
Hang a view in the foyer with its reader and the maker’s slip.

dialogue.speaker: stage-director
dialogue.text: A keeper says, ‘Leave it by the door.’ A worker at the threshold replies, ‘I can wait.’ Between them the keeper moves a crate and the room goes quiet for a beat. Run our two rehearsals. Keep the words in place and see where your eye goes.

dialogue.speaker: stage-director
dialogue.text: The printer’s draft says the worker has a new line. Both rehearsals end with ‘I can wait.’ The line stays put. It is the silence that moves around the crate move. How should we mark the change for the cast?

options.text: Circle the pause on both cue sheets and keep the lines where they are.
Set the two movement marks beside each other on the rehearsal board.
Give me another moment with the scene.

dialogue.speaker: stage-director
dialogue.text: The cast can see where the quiet beat falls and practise both versions. One actor felt the pause put the worker in the foreground. Another watched the keeper. I’ll leave space for both readings.

dialogue.speaker: stage-director
dialogue.text: A pair of marks makes the order visible. The actors still hear the same words. I’ll keep the blocking plan nearby so they can check what actually moves.

dialogue.speaker: stage-director
dialogue.text: Take the rehearsal notes to Hari. Some audience seats see the edges of our stage. Their view can change which beat they notice first.

dialogue.speaker: stage-director
dialogue.text: The cast kept its lines and movement. Hari has recorded where a person watching from the side might lose sight of the crate. I’ll use that when we arrange the next scene.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: People at the front see both actors and the full crate move. A post changes what people at the side can see. Check the blocking plan in rehearsal and our view note here. We hear the same dialogue from both.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: On these boards the company calls the crate mark a cue. Regulars in the side seats know that they can follow a missed move by listening for its rhythm. New audience members may only hear a silence. Which view would you put beside the cast’s plan?

options.text: Keep a front-seat view with the full move visible.
Keep the side view beside the lines the audience can still hear.
I’ll look through both seats again.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: I’ll keep the front view and add the post at the edge of the picture. A visitor can see why a neighbour heard the same words and missed part of the move.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: The side seats have a place on our board now. I’ll add the front view beside them. Together the two notes show what people in either seat can follow.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: Both views are here. Ask Edda to compare the rehearsals before we set a cue order. A good staging can hold two readings at once.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: The hall is filling. We can hold the audience with the worker at the threshold, or let the crate move catch their eye first. The company will use either cue order and keep the same words.

options.text: Stage the silence before the keeper moves the crate.
Stage the crate move before the silence.
Keep the stage open a little longer.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: The company holds still for a beat. From the front row, a reader is watching the worker by the door. Then the crate moves and the worker replies. Someone in the gallery stays behind after the scene.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: The crate moves beside the door before the quiet beat. A reader in the front follows it, then looks back at the worker. From the side, someone has heard the reply and wants to talk.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: A note has appeared in the gallery. A reader asks why the worker waited. Go and see how they heard the scene.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: From the side a reader heard the waiting line and took the earlier silence for a refusal. The program can say where we placed the pause and what the side seat could see. The keeper’s reason can stay open.

options.text: Add the pause cue and side-seat view to tonight’s program.
I’ll return to the gallery first.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: The first row saw the crate move and called the silence a welcome. The side seats heard the same reply without the same view. Put our move and silence in the program and leave both readers room to compare.

options.text: Add the movement cue and the two views to tonight’s program.
I’ll check the sightline again.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: The reader has moved nearer the front for the next show. They want to see the crate move after the pause. I’ve written that question beside the cue, where the actors can find it.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: A reader in the side seats says the movement cue will help them compare the scene with the front row. The notes name the move. The two groups can still disagree about the keeper’s reason.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: Our understudy helped put the benches back. They missed one rehearsal. A cue sheet could let them follow the cast’s work and try the other timing on their own.

options.text: Leave the understudy a large cue copy with both orders.
Take the doorstep question back to the City of Copies.
I’ll take another look at the hall.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: The understudy can check the spoken line, move and silent beat from the bench. I’ll mark the two orders as alternatives and keep tonight’s program with them.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: Mina mentioned the people who waited outside her reading hall. Our program can show a move and a pause. A signed register could tell us a doorway rule. See what Mina’s clerk has signed, then decide where to put a copy.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The trial log tells us about the queue on Tuesday. The admission register gives the hall’s rule. Watch a person at the door and you could still guess wrong about why they’re waiting. Which copy would help them check the rule?

options.text: Post the signed admission line at the door, where readers decide whether to enter.
Send the rule and the slip’s purpose to the returns queue.
Leave the register open for now.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The door copy says readers can enter with or without a return slip. It names the signed admission register. Someone can check the stated rule before deciding whether to go in.

dialogue.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
dialogue.text: The queue copy says a slip identifies the item coming back. It also carries the signed entry rule. A reader can leave the return queue and go inside without one.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: Hari holds up the printer’s call slip. It says ‘The keeper refuses entry.’ By that post, you can hear ‘I can wait’ and still miss part of the crate move. ‘The touring players give a spoken call before the first line. Here we leave that beat quiet and pass slips along the low rail. I can change what we put into people’s hands or ears. Which shall we use?’

options.text: Give Hari a spoken cue that reaches the back. Use the quiet beat to tell listeners where the post hides the move.
Clip a sightline slip to the low rail. Keep the opening quiet and ask the near bench to pass the cue along.
Leave the slip here while I take another look.

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: Hari strikes the test bell and says, ‘Watch the threshold. From beside the post, part of the crate move is hidden.’ An actor holds their first line until his voice drops. Hari nods towards the back bench. ‘Find out what carried that far.’

dialogue.speaker: stage-host
dialogue.text: You clip the slip to the rail. ‘Beside the post, part of the crate move is hidden. The words carry past it.’ Hari gives the first line its quiet opening. The near bench lifts the slip from its clip. ‘See how far they pass it.’

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A visitor has left a folded note asking for one aisle seat near the door. She gives no reason. At this house an usher can hold a place with a ribbon until the opening bell. The folded note can stay at the desk.

options.text: Keep the folded request at the usher’s desk.
Leave the folded note on its hook.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The usher records which seat is being asked for. A ribbon can name the place and when the hold ends. People in the queue can read that much.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The queue post is on a movable foot. A visitor who waits beside it can read the tall programme, but the queue hides the low seat map. Touring groups mark the queue on the wall before they choose their own seats, so everyone in turn can see the map.

options.text: Check where the post can stand without covering the seat map.
Leave the post at its old mark.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The wall mark leaves a path to the low map. Walkers can read the map as they reach the front of the queue. The post on stage is a different one. The scenery stays where the actors set it.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: Two regulars are waiting in order. One wants to keep her place in the queue while the visitor waits by the door. The visitor wants to know where she can sit. You have room to keep the aisle clear either way. Which arrangement should the usher use for this performance?

options.text: Reserve the aisle place until the opening bell. Put the queue by the wall.
Move the queue post to the wall. Let visitors choose their places in order.
Leave the seating decision with the usher for now.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A ribbon on the aisle seat gives the visitor a place before she joins the room. The notice tells the regulars which other seats are open. If she leaves it unused when the first bell goes, the usher will offer it to the queue. The folded request stays at the desk.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The post moves to the wall. Everyone has a turn at the low map before the line moves. When her turn comes, the visitor points to the unclaimed aisle seat. She has room to explain what seat she wants without opening her note for the room.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The paper scene shows a person with a basket just outside a doorway. Both the figure and the door are fixed to the panel. The same lamp fits a low bracket to the side and a stand facing the panel. Change the light and look at what the visitor notices.

options.text: Lower the lamp into the side bracket.
Set the lamp to face the relief.
Set a first look for the next visitor.
Set a first look for the next visitor.
Leave the lighting as it is.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The side lamp stretches the figure’s shadow across the step. The basket and the person are still on their original marks. The relief is ready beside the bracket.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The shadow draws closer to the figure. You can see the hand on the basket strap and where the paper coat is creased. Nothing on the panel moved. Look at this view from the same place.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The keeper wants a relief for people waiting in the foyer. The maker’s slip records the time of this rehearsal. Nobody has a dated account of the event in the scene. You can show what one reader felt and which part of the work helped them feel it.

options.text: Hang the side-lit relief with the visitor’s account of hesitation.
Hang the front-lit relief with the reader’s account of care.
Keep both views at the rehearsal bench for now.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The foyer copy keeps the long shadow. A visitor pauses when the shaded strip crosses the doorway. She says she can feel a wait before the next step. The handbill names the light and the rehearsal. The arrival date remains open. A later visitor asks if you can show the rehearsal relief when you go back.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The foyer copy keeps the shorter shadow. A reader follows the arm to the basket. She says the grip looks like care for what is inside it. The handbill keeps that reading beside the maker’s dated note. Nobody adds a date for the arrival. A later visitor asks if you can show the rehearsal relief when you go back.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The visitor stays in the doorway for a full breath. “I keep waiting for the paper foot to rise.” She traces the edge in the air, then lifts the handbill on her way out.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The shadow covers the step from here. The visitor leans far enough to see the lamp and the same paper foot together.

options.text: Bring the light round to the front.
Leave this first position for a longer look.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The visitor watches the shadow shorten without the figure moving. Then she follows the crease in the paper hand. “I thought their arm was empty. What are they trying so hard to carry?”

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The next visitor has time for one look at the rehearsal relief. The copy you hung in the foyer can stay where it is. You can let the first view stand for a moment, or let the visitor watch you change the light.

options.text: Leave the side lamp for a quiet first look.
Put the side lamp where the visitor can see how it casts the long shadow.
Leave the rehearsal relief as it is for now.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The visitor follows the bent arm to the basket. “Look how tight they’re holding it. I want to hear what’s inside before the door opens.” He reads the handbill after a long look at the grip.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The bent paper arm lies in the light. The visitor shifts farther back so he can watch the arm and the lamp together.

options.text: Move the lamp into the side bracket.
Leave this first position for a longer look.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The visitor sees the grip fade while the long shadow reaches the step. “The paper foot is still fixed there. How can I feel the wait more from here?” He takes a step sideways to see where the shadow ends.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The next visitor has time for one look at the rehearsal relief. The copy you hung in the foyer can stay where it is. You can let the first view stand for a moment, or let the visitor watch you change the light.

options.text: Leave the front lamp for a quiet first look.
Put the front lamp where the visitor can see it pick out the grip.
Leave the rehearsal relief as it is for now.

dialogue.speaker: vesper-quill
dialogue.text: An usher has time for one line before the bell. “The keeper refused the worker.” That will get a latecomer looking in the right direction. I wish a whole page could be said in one breath. Put your cue beside mine and let the foyer hear it.

options.text: Bring the rehearsal and usher’s notes to the programme stand.
Leave the foyer with the revised programme as it is.

dialogue.speaker: vesper-quill
dialogue.text: One line, and a whole foyer to see what it did. You ought to see another line the Nexus hung up. Ask Ise about Harrowmere. I won’t keep your usher waiting.

hints.text: A new passage has opened.
Someone at the theatre wants to see what two audiences hear in one line.
Return to the Nexus after marking where both surveys stopped.
Follow the passage to the House of Performance. The foyer leads to rehearsal and the gallery.
One beat changes place. Keep the lines in view.
The silence can come before or after the same movement.
At the rehearsal table, watch the pause-first and move-first versions to the end.
Talk to Edda after advancing all four cues in both versions. Choose how you want the cast to compare the two.
An audience can hear a scene it only partly sees.
The blocking plan follows the actors. The gallery note says which seats can follow the move.
Read the blocking plan in rehearsal and the sightline note in the gallery.
Talk to Hari about whose view the crew should prepare for. The two notes belong to different parts of the show.
Both cue orders tell the same short scene. Each points the eye somewhere first.
A pause before the crate move holds attention on the waiting worker. A move first makes the action easier to notice.
Ask Hari to call the cue order once rehearsal and both view notes are ready.
Keep the pause first or move the crate first. The actor will keep both spoken lines.
Someone stayed behind to ask about the keeper.
Look for the audience note in the gallery.
Read what the audience member heard the worker say.
Keep what the audience saw and heard separate from what it took the keeper to mean.
The keeper moves a crate. The keeper’s reason remains open.
Use the blocking plan and the side seats’ view to talk about the audience’s reading.
Take the audience note to Hari after the performance.
Add a cue note to the program for tonight’s order. Give the audience its question without turning it into a fact.
The understudy needs a record of the order, words and movement.
Leave the silent beat clearly named on the page.
Speak with Hari after the program update.
Ask for a larger cue sheet so another performer can rehearse either arrangement.
Think about what could state a doorway rule rather than report a queue.
A trial log and a signed register serve different purposes.
Return to the City of Copies. Look in the Record Room for the admission register.
Read the signed admission register. It gives the current entrance rule and the purpose of a return slip.
There are readers at the door and people waiting in the returns queue.
Place the rule where one of those groups is deciding what to do.
Take the signed register’s line to the admission desk on the landing.
Choose a copy for the hall door or a note for the return queue. Both keep the rule and the source.
A seat can lose the move and still hear the words.
Use the post mark on the sightline note. The two benches can still hear ‘I can wait.’
Keep the cue within what the bench can check. Decide whether Hari should speak it or the bench should pass it.
Set one cue at the stand. Check the back bench if Hari spoke, or the far end of the low rail if the slip travelled.
A person looking for a place may need to see something the queue hides.
The request tells you what place is needed. The post helps you see how people can get there.
The folded slip is just to the left of the gallery arrival. The movable post is on the other side of the aisle.
Keep the folded request at the desk and test the wall mark for the queue post.
Think about what the public needs to know before it can wait or choose.
A held seat gives certainty early. An open queue can let people choose after everyone has a view of the plan.
Use the usher’s desk near the gallery entrance after checking the request and the post.
Name the seat and time of a hold, or move the queue to the wall so visitors can use the low map. Read the resulting notice.
A shadow can move even when the thing casting it stays still.
Try both places for the lamp. Find the maker’s slip to see which time it records.
The lantern bracket and relief face the lower bench in rehearsal. Read the maker’s slip east of them.
Choose the side bracket and look at the relief. Choose the front stand and look again. Read the slip beside the bench.
A reader’s experience has a place beside the work.
One visitor noticed the long shadow. One noticed the grip on the basket. Both can support a display.
Use the foyer proof stand after recording both views and checking the maker’s date.
Send either lit view with one reader’s account. Look for the resulting relief in the foyer.

journal.title: The doorway pause
journal.text: The cast spoke the same lines and moved the same crate in both rehearsals. I chose where to place the pause, then helped the gallery describe the cue and the views without assigning the keeper a reason.

journal.title: A copy for the understudy
journal.text: Hari and I separated the lines, move and pause on a larger cue sheet. The next performer can try either order.

journal.title: A rule by the door
journal.text: A pause gave the theatre audience room to wonder why a person waited. The lending register answered a different question. It gave the hall’s entry rule, which we could carry as a signed line to people at the door or queue.
I helped Hari send a cue about what the post hid and checked who received it. The cue left each listener room to hear a different reason in the same line.
The ribbon and the moving queue post give a visitor different ways to find a place. The public notice says how the seats work. The folded request tells the usher only what seat was asked for.

One light gave the paper figure a long shadow, and the other let a reader see the grip on the basket. Both readers had something they could point to. The maker’s slip dated the rehearsal, while the event in the relief kept its open date.
The visitor had a moment with the first lighting before opening the handbill. They asked about a movement or an object that the maker has left off the page.
We kept the paper figure fixed and showed the next visitor what moving the light did. They asked about something that had only just caught their eye.

moments.did: You compared how the scene looked from two seats and left room for different readings.
You left a working cue sheet for an understudy who missed rehearsal.
You checked how a visitor could reach the aisle and protected their folded request while arranging the queue.
moments.prompt: Which part of the seating rule helps a person who arrives after the room is half full?

moments.did: You changed the light, listened to two readings of the same figure and kept the maker’s date with the account you shared.
moments.prompt: What might another person see in the same view?

cards.title: Edda’s two rehearsal orders
cards.text: The keeper moves the crate and the worker says “I can wait” in both rehearsals. Edda moves the silence from before the crate move to after it.
cards.limits: The cue sheet records timing, words and movements. It leaves each character’s motive open.

cards.title: Hari’s two seat views
cards.text: The crate move is clear from the front bench. A post cuts off part of the view from the side seats. Both audiences hear the same words.
cards.limits: The two accounts cover those positions and this rehearsal.

cards.title: The usher’s quick call
cards.text: At the opening bell an usher called “Watch the doorway.” A late arrival turned to the doorway before the keeper moved the crate.
cards.limits: The usher saw one person turn towards the scene. It gives no account of what that person thought happened.

showdowns.title: One Line Before the Bell
showdowns.intro: A late arrival is still looking for a seat. Hari lays the revised programme down. Vesper pins a short line beside it.

opponentClaim.text: Tell everyone the keeper refused the worker. Anyone who saw the scene can see that much.

links.text: The pause fixes what the keeper meant.
links.cracked: Two rehearsals use the same words and move. Moving the silence changes what an audience may read into it.
links.holds: This card does not compare the two orders of the silence.

links.text: Every seat saw the same movement.
links.cracked: The side post hides part of the move. The view from the front cannot stand in for the view from the side.
links.holds: This card does not tell us what a person behind the post could see.

counterexamples.why: One side reader missed part of the crate move. That reader could hear the wait without seeing all of its movement.

opponentClaim.narrowed: The keeper moves the crate beside the doorway. The wait is part of the scene.
opponentClaim.sourceReply: Vesper taps the short card. “I sat in the front. I saw the move. I heard someone behind me ask which part they should look at.”

playerClaims.text: Call “Watch the doorway.” A late arrival can find the scene and read the fuller note when they sit.

supports.why: The late reader turned to the doorway at the simple call.
The post gives a reason to keep a separate note for the reader in the side seats.

playerClaims.reframe: A notice can help a visitor find a moment. The rehearsal can show what moved and when. Those are two jobs.

playerClaims.text: Give the crate move and silence their own lines, and mark the view from the side.

supports.why: The two orders keep words and movement fixed while placing the silence on different sides of the move.
The side post explains why those seats need a line that keeps the visible limit.

playerClaims.reframe: A witness can tell us where the crate went and what their seat hid. The character’s reason is another question.

witnesses.name: Host Hari
witnesses.line: A side reader asked whether the worker wanted to wait. I could show what our post hid and give the two cues their own lines.

fairPoints.text: Vesper says, “At the bell an usher has one breath. A visitor needs a line they can act on.”
fairPoints.concede: You keep the short call. Hari leaves a place beside it for the fuller scene note.

script.line: Vesper asks which record an usher ought to be able to show.
Vesper points to the board. “What did the side seats have to go on?”

exposed.text: The audience asks Hari to take down the refusal caption. The two seat drawings go where it hung. Vesper lifts the pin and bows.

narrowed.text: Vesper crosses out “refused” and leaves the crate move on the card. Hari pins it beside the cue order.

won-over.text: Vesper offers “Watch the doorway.” Hari puts the short call above the side-seat note. Vesper bows to the waiting usher.

split.text: Some ask for the short call. Others want to see the seat drawings first. Hari leaves two stacks on the foyer stand.

lost-ground.text: Several arrivals take Vesper’s first card into the gallery. Hari leaves the checked scene note next to the remaining copies. A side reader goes back for it.
